overview.text: The Cyrus Cylinder is a clay foundation inscription written in Akkadian cuneiform after the Persian king Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE. Its text presents a Babylonian account of conquest: it says the god Marduk chose Cyrus, criticizes the previous king Nabonidus, and describes restoring temples and returning displaced divine images and people. The cylinder was discovered at Babylon in 1879. Although sometimes called an ancient charter of human rights, it is better understood in the tradition of Mesopotamian royal inscriptions, which proclaimed a ruler's legitimacy and piety. Its claims show how Cyrus presented his rule to Babylonian audiences, not a neutral record of every policy he carried out.

key_facts.text: The inscription is in Akkadian cuneiform on a clay cylinder.
It was found at Babylon in 1879.
The text connects Cyrus's capture of Babylon with the god Marduk's favor.
It describes temple restoration and the return of displaced gods and people as royal claims.

overview.text: On 28 October 312 CE, Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius near the Milvian Bridge outside Rome. The victory left Constantine in control of the Roman Empire's western territories. Christian writers later linked the campaign to a divine sign: Lactantius described a dream before the battle, while Eusebius gave a more elaborate account of a vision. Their accounts differ, so the details should be treated as reported traditions rather than an independently observed event. Constantine went on to favor Christianity and, with Licinius, adopted a policy of religious toleration in 313. The battle mattered both for imperial power and for the later history of Christianity.

overview.text: Columbus's first Atlantic voyage reached the Caribbean in 1492 under the sponsorship of Spain's monarchs. At Guanahani in the Bahamas, he encountered Taíno people, whose communities already had developed farming, navigation, religious, and political traditions. Columbus claimed islands for Ferdinand and Isabella and reported the journey in a letter circulated in Europe in 1493. He believed the islands belonged to Asia and later made three more Caribbean voyages. The expedition began sustained contact between Europeans and Indigenous peoples of the Americas; that contact led to colonization and devastating disease and exploitation for many Native communities. The Taíno were participants in this history, not a backdrop to European exploration.

overview.text: Jamal Khashoggi was a Saudi journalist whose writing criticized restrictions on expression in Saudi Arabia. On 2 October 2018, Saudi agents killed him inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul, during a visit there. His death brought worldwide attention to the safety of journalists and to accountability for state violence. A 2021 United States intelligence assessment concluded that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman approved an operation to capture or kill Khashoggi; that conclusion is an assessment by the U.S. intelligence community. Khashoggi's final Washington Post column argued for a freer press in the Arab world. His case remains a prominent example of the risks faced by dissident reporters.

overview.text: Wilhelm II was German emperor and king of Prussia from 1888 until his abdication in November 1918. During the July Crisis of 1914, he exchanged personal telegrams with Russia's Tsar Nicholas II, often called the “Willy–Nicky” telegrams. The messages discussed the conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia, Russian military preparations, and the danger of a wider European war. Their personal appeals did not stop the escalation. During World War I, German military leaders increasingly directed operations and policy, reducing the emperor's practical influence. When revolution accompanied Germany's defeat in 1918, Wilhelm abdicated and went into exile in the Netherlands, ending the German Empire's monarchy.

overview.text: The University of Bologna grew from a medieval community of scholars in the Italian city of Bologna. Its conventional founding year is 1088, a retrospective date rather than a precisely documented opening day. The institution is widely described as the oldest university in the Western world. Legal study, especially Roman law, was central to its early reputation, and students organized themselves in associations that shaped the university's governance. Its history shows how medieval learning developed through teachers, students, and city life rather than through a single founding decree. Later scholars associated with Bologna include physicist Laura Bassi, whose eighteenth-century career challenged restrictions on women's academic roles.

overview.text: The Duvalier dynasty ruled Haiti from 1957 to 1986 through two presidents from the same family. François Duvalier, known as “Papa Doc,” won the presidency in 1957 and built a repressive personal regime that used the Tontons Macoutes militia to intimidate opponents. Before his death in 1971, constitutional changes prepared the way for his son Jean-Claude, “Baby Doc,” to succeed him. Jean-Claude maintained authoritarian rule, even as members of his circle accumulated wealth amid widespread poverty. Public opposition grew in the 1980s, and he fled Haiti in February 1986. The family's long rule left a legacy of political violence and weakened civic institutions in Haiti.

overview.text: On 14 July 1789, Parisians attacked the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, during the opening crisis of the French Revolution. Crowds had obtained firearms elsewhere in the city and sought the gunpowder stored at the fortress. After fighting, its defenders surrendered and the crowd freed seven prisoners. The small number of captives mattered less than the Bastille's symbolic association with arbitrary royal power. News of its fall showed that urban crowds could shape events alongside the newly assembled national representatives. The date later became part of France's national commemoration, although the 14 July holiday also recalls the Fête de la Fédération held a year later.

overview.text: Haile Selassie I, born Tafari Makonnen, became emperor of Ethiopia in 1930 and ruled until 1974. He pursued reforms and represented Ethiopia internationally, and helped establish African cooperation. Addis Ababa became the headquarters of the Organization of African Unity during his reign. His government also drew criticism for failing to address severe poverty and famine. In 1974 a military coup removed him; he died under house arrest the following year. For many adherents of Rastafari, a movement that arose in Jamaica, Haile Selassie holds sacred or messianic significance. That religious understanding should be attributed to Rastafari believers, rather than imposed as a historical fact about him.

overview.text: Ur was a major Sumerian city in southern Mesopotamia, in the area of present-day Iraq. Its rulers helped build the state known as the Third Dynasty of Ur around the end of the third millennium BCE. King Ur-Nammu began the great stepped temple platform, or ziggurat, associated with the moon god Nanna. The city's importance also appears in its Royal Cemetery, excavated in the twentieth century, where elaborate graves contained jewelry, musical instruments, and other objects. Archaeologists use those finds to study wealth, ritual, and social hierarchy in ancient Mesopotamia. Ur's ancient relationship to the Euphrates should not be confused with the river's present course or today's coastline.
